analysis:
The PR is documentation-only: it adds a section to docs/reference/protocol-messages.md (head lines 202-219, "Close codes and the reconnect wait"). The supplied units are base-side text of later parts of the file (base lines 956-1586), which the change does not touch. I examined them as surrounding context only.

The added text describes provider behavior in CoordinatorReconnectPolicy. A WebSocket close code of 1012 draws the next wait from serviceRestartDelayRange without growing the backoff. Any other close code, or no close frame, uses ExponentialBackoff, which grows. A session stable for stableSessionDuration, counted from its register frame, resets the backoff. The provider ignores the close reason. Every reconnect sends a fresh register.

Security relevance (TB-002, A-018, A-008):
- The close code comes from the trusted coordinator side, so no new adversarial input path is introduced.
- The doc states that every reconnect sends a fresh register, so reconnection still goes through the full registration, attestation and App Attest flow. Nothing indicates that T-053 (stale authorization surviving a connection change) or the T-052 gating is weakened.
- A network attacker who can inject a close frame, or a compromised endpoint, could induce a short fixed 1012 delay instead of growing backoff. That is a reconnect-storm risk to the coordinator. It is bounded by the delay range, whose values are not supplied. The code is not changed here, and the transport is TLS, which I assume without evidence. This is a possible availability follow-up in the policy code, not a finding on this doc diff.

Unverified contracts: I could not see CoordinatorReconnectPolicy.swift or the runtime-constants values. I could not confirm that the doc matches the implementation, or that serviceRestartDelayRange is jittered and nonzero. The statement that older providers treat 1012 like any other close is also unverified.

No security controls change and no threat-model assumption is invalidated, so there are no findings.
